text: Electroless-plated cobalt alloys with tungsten typically exceeding 5 at.% are the common barrier materials for copper metallization. As cobalt is a new interconnect material for advanced microchips, it is worth studying the advanced cobalt-interconnect metallization process that involves extremely diluted cobalt-tungsten (CoW) alloys with an eliminated impurity resistivity and enhanced electromigration reliability. To this aim, we fabricated three different CoW nanolines with 0.03, 0.06 and 0.11 at.% of W using an electroless process, and examined their electromigration behaviors under accelerated stressing conditions, using Co lines as a control. All three W contents, especially 0.06 at.%, mitigate Co electromigration. The mechanism for the electromigration mitigation is due to an improvement of the film s nanomechanical and surface wetting properties, as well as grain-structure refinements. A full account of the relationship between the film properties, grain structures and electromigration testing results is given, reasonably explaining the cause of the reliability optimization.

text: The contact critical dimension of the CMOS transistors currently using copper (Cu) as a core interconnect material is expected to reach 18 nm [1], associated with a diminishment of interconnect width towards less than a few tens of nm. The rather long electron mean free path of 40 nm for Cu would induce multiple electron scatterings in such narrow lines, giving rise to a high residual electrical resistivity [2]. Therefore, Cu is not a good interconnect conductor for future technology nodes. Compared to Cu, cobalt (Co) has a much shorter electron mean free path of about 9 nm, leading to the product of the resistivity and mean free path of Co being less than that of Cu: 6.0 5 × 1 0 ^ - 1 6 vs. 6.7 0×10^-16Ωm^2 [2]. Considering the resistivity-size effect, Co is considered to be a more appropriate interconnect material than Cu, especially as the line width (or cross section) is reduced down to below a crossover value of about 15 nm [3–5] (or 450 nm 2) [6,7]. Moreover, electromigration is essentially a forced metal diffusion behavior and the key factor that influences the electromigration reliability of a conductive line is the magnitude of its effective valence (Z*) and diffusivity (D): the lower the product of the Z ^ * and D, the higher the electromigration reliability. The absolute value of the Z ^ * for Co is about 5 to 10 times lower than that of Cu [8,9]. With a higher melting point of 1495 ◦C than 1085 ◦C of Cu, Co has a much lower (about one order of magnitude) self-diffusivity than Cu [10]. Indeed, the product of the Z* and D for Co is two orders of magnitude smaller than that of Cu [11,12]. Therefore, Co has become the new, alternative interconnection material for advanced microchips [1].

text: Electroless process has long been used to prepare thin barrier/cap layers of Co alloys for Cu-interconnect metallization [13]. The basic components in an electroless cobalt-alloy plating solution are typically cobalt sulfate (CoSO_4) as a source of Co ions and dimethylamine borane (C_2H_9BN), sodium hydroborate (NaBH) or sodium hypophosphite (NaH_2PO_2) as a chemical reductant. The oxidation of the chemical reductant results in the incorporation of boron or phosphors into the deposited Co, creating a solute-strengthening effect that stabilizes the phase structure, stuffs grain boundaries and/or generates an amorphous matrix, which are all beneficial to barrier/cap properties. Moreover, as a refractory metal, tungsten (W) is highly resistant to heat and abrasion. Its addition to the binary Co alloys thus further elevates thermal-mechanical and barrier properties. Therefore, innovate formulations based on sulfate baths with an added W-containing salt, such as tungstate [ 1 4, 1 5 ] or phosphotungstic acid [16], have been developed to fabricate barrier/cap layers of ternary Co alloys with high W contents usually exceeding 5 at.%.

text: To serve as a core-conducting interconnect material, thin metal films need to have an electrical resistivity close to their bulk values. However, high concentrations of alloy components, particularly heavy elements such as W, in thin films of binary or ternary cobalt-based alloys would induce a high impurity electrical resistivity. After thermal annealing, the tungsten-added cobalt binary/ternary films still give a high resistivity value exceeding several tens or even hundreds of μΩ-cm [17,18]. We have recently developed an all-wet self-assembled-monolayer (SAM) seeding and electroless process for cobalt metallization. By using a CoSO _ 4 -N _2H_4 (hydrazine; a metal-free reductant) bath, thin films and nanolines of alloy-free Co with (after annealing) a low resistivity of≤15 μΩ-cm are fabricated [19]. In this study, we report an extension of our previous work by adding tungstate to the CoSO _4–N_2H_4 bath for the interconnect metallization of various Co alloys with trace W contents (termed CoW) of 0.03, 0.06 and 0.11 at.%, giving a low impurity-component resistivity potentially suitable for future interconnect-material applications. By using unalloyed Co as a reference, the enhancement of the electromigration reliability of interconnect lines of the various CoW alloys, in particular with 0.06 at.% added W, will be confirmed. The correlation between nanomechanical/wetting properties of the surface films and the difference in electromigration failure profiles and grain structures of the interconnect lines will be analyzed, elucidating why the optimal W content (0.06 at.%) gives the greatest effectiveness of mitigating electromigration failure.

text: Prior to electromigration testing, the samples of Co,CoW_l,CoW_m and CoW lines were annealed (400\^°C/30 min) using an Ulvac’s Mila-5000 rapid thermal vacuum annealer. All annealing treatments were performed in flowing Ar -H_2 (5 %) that prevented the samples from oxidation. A heating rate of 15~^°C~s^-1 was used and fast cooling was performed by simply switching off the heating. They were then placed on a thermal chuck situated in a probe-station-enclosed dark box, immediately under constant current stressing by using a Keithley 4200- SCS semiconductor parameter analyzer. text: Nanomechanical scratch testing of thin films of Co, CoW_l,CoW_m and CoW_h was conducted in a Bruker’s Hysitron TI 980 Tribolndenter. The Tribolndenter was equipped with two sensors for precise force and depth measurements using a state-of-the-art piezoelectric actuator. This advanced design allowed us to control each and every measurement by progressively increasing the normal load of a diamond stylus in a controlled fashion, while synchronously collecting the feedback data of normal displacement, lateral force and lateral displacement. Subsequently, the related plots were automatically generated by using a Hysitron TriboScan software. On-site scanning probe microscopical imaging of the whole scratch profile for the feedback of the scratch data was used to derive the nanomechanical properties of the tested films, such as critical load, delamination force, adhesion strength and friction coefficient.

text: When adsorbed onto the deposit surface, W (VI) ions tend to become an inhibiting component that blocks the self-catalytic sites of Co [25]. Thus, the W (VI) ions depress Co deposition and their reduction reaction into metallic W being incorporated to the main Co deposit is interde pendent upon the main reduction reaction of the cobaltous ions. Specifically, previous studies have shown that adding high contents of tungstate ( WO_3^4+) to the cobalt sulfate ( Co ^ 2 +) aqueous solutions with WO _ 3 ^ 4 + -to-CO ^ 2 + molarity ratios exceeding 0.3 or even greater than 2, using a given chemical reductant such as hypophosphite or dimethylamine borane, results in a decrease in the deposition rates of Co [25–28]. Here, the pure Co film was deposited by a sulfate-citrate-hydrazine bath. It should be noted that the concentration of the sulfate in this bath was 0.2 M. The CoW_l,CoW_m and CoW_h films were deposited by otherwise this same bath except including quite low tungstate concentrations of about 2.5 0 × 1 0 ^ - 4, 1.0 6 × 1 0 ^ - 3 and 5.3 0 × 1 0 ^ - 3 M, respectively. These results suggest that the tungstate in the tungstate-diluted Co-plating baths also depresses Co deposition as it does in the tungstate-concentrated baths.

text: Thin films of binary cobalt alloys, such as Co(P) or Co(B), are typically deposited by aqueous electrolytes that contain cobalt sulfate, hypophosphite (or borazane) and a citrate chelating agent. Tungstate, as used in this study, is usually added to the above electroless baths for the incorporation of metallic W into the binary alloys for barrier/cap applications. Traditionally, highly concentrated tungstate, in terms of tungstate-to-cobalt sulfate (or $\mathsf { \bar { W } O _ { 3 } ^ { 4 + } - t o - C O ^ { 2 + } } )$ molarity ratios of 0.3 or greater, is used, which results in the incorporation of substantial amounts of metallic W in the range of 2 10 at.% to the Co matrix. In spite of the fact that pure W cannot be deposited by either chemical or electrochemical methods, electrochemical studies suggest that Co serves as a catalyst for the electroless deposition of W; namely, after the deposition of Co on catalytic particles or layers, the deposited Co subsequently serves as another catalyst to activate the codeposition of Co and W. The W can be reduced from tungstile ions $( \mathrm { W O } _ { 2 } ^ { 2 + } )$ , and is then simultaneously incorporated into the Co matrix during the reduction of the cobaltous ions via a so-called induced codeposition mechanism [16, 28,29]. Here, the baths with extremely low tungstate–to–cobalt sulfate molarity ratios of $1 . 2 0 \times 1 0 ^ { - 3 } , 5 . 3 0 \times 1 0 ^ { - 3 }$ and $\overline { { 2 . 6 5 \times 1 0 ^ { - 2 } } }$ were used to deposit CoW alloys, and the deposited films indeed contained only 0.03, 0.06 and 0.11 atomic percentage of $\mathsf { W } ,$ , respectively. This result suggests that, for the cobalt-tungsten alloy films deposited by the tungstate-diluted hydrazine baths, the trace W contents are incorporated to the Co film matrixes also via the induced codeposition mechanism, as for the conventional tungstate-concentrated baths. Indeed, the study of the deposition and film properties of tungsten-containing binary/ternary alloys of Co using $\mathrm { C o S O } _ { 4 } { \mathrm { - N } } _ { 2 } \mathrm { H } _ { 4 }$ bath formulations with diluted tungsten-ion sources is rather limited. The mechanism for plating diluted cobalt-tungsten alloys using the tungstate-diluted baths is worthy of investigation via electrochemical analysis. This topic is behind the scope of this current study, and a detailed electrochemical investigation will be made in a separate project which will be presented elsewhere.

text: The seeding process used in this study is capable of loading 2-nm sized catalytic particles onto the substrates of SAM-coated SiO _2/Si [22], which are the catalytic sites for the electroless growth of W-alloyed Co or unalloyed Co. During the course of electroless deposition, the W-added Co or Co deposits surrounding the 2 nm-sized catalytic particles are expanded with plating time to become island-like deposits, eventually coalescing themselves into a thin continuous film. As demonstrated by the top-view and cross-sectional (inset) SEM micrographs in Fig. 3a and 3b, respectively, the thin Co and CoW_m films yield similar uniform surface morphologies and microstructures. The two Co and CoW_m films were further annealed to a certain extent (500~^°C/30 min in flowing Ar/H 2 gas), and the associated top-view SEM micrographs are shown in Fig. 3c and 3d, respectively. It can be seen from Fig. 3c that the annealing causes a serious disruption and agglomeration of the Co film, leading to the exposure of the underlying dielectric substrate. However, an identical annealing induces densification and substantial grain growth of the CoW_m film, which still retains an intact film structure (Fig. 3d). These findings suggest that the Co film is strengthened by the extremely diluted alloying of 0.06 at.% W.

text: The samples for nanoscratch testing were thin films of Co, CoW_l CoW_m and CoW_h on the same SAM-tethered SiO _ 2 on Si. These films had the same thickness of 70 nm. Their nanomechanical properties were measured by nanoscratch testing using a diamond stylus to draw across the film surfaces at a constant speed ( 0.6 ~ μ m ~ s ^ - 1) with progressively increased normal forces towards a maximum predetermined force. Considering the difference in film hardness and adhesion strength, the normal force was increased at a constant rate of 10μNs^-1 and 15 μNs^-1 for the Co/CoW_l films and the CoW_m/CoW_h films, respectively. The typical sets of the plots of lateral force versus ramped normal force obtained from a single scratch of these surface films are given in Fig. 6a and b for thin films of Co/CoW_l and CoW_m/CoW_h, respectively. The progressive increase in the applied normal force results in a gradual increase in the force that acts in the direction parallel to the coating surfaces, known as the lateral force. When the scratch just penetrates any of these four films, a sharp change in the friction coefficient occurs. This moment is associated with fluctuations in the lateral force, used to define the critical applied load for film delamination. Due to the subtle nature of fluctuations in the lateral forces responsible for film delamination, the black straight lines in Fig. 6a and b serve as the fitting curves which facilitate the identification of the critical applied loads for the four surface films. Here, three meaningful scratches were made for each surface film, from which the average critical load with a standard deviation for film delamination was obtained, As shown in the bar graph of Fig. 6c, the critical loads of the Co,CoW_l,CoW_m and CoW_h films are 1466 ± 134 μN, 1811 ± 99 μN, 2266 ± 96 μN and 2115 ± 165 μ N, respectively.

text: The values of the adhesion strength, hardness, specific surface energy and electromigration mean time to failure (MTF) of Co, CoW l, CoW_m and CoW_h, as obtained from the preceding sections, are compiled in Table 2 for comparison. According to this table, the extension of the lifetime and reduction in the scaling factor of Co by W alloying correlate closely with the improvement of surface and nanomechanical properties of the thin films. Notably, surface energy is an important thermodynamic factor that decides the wettability of a condensed matter to a heterogeneous supporting substrate. The deposited film with a lower surface energy would have a higher wetting tendency and thus should be with a greater substrate adherence than the counterpart with a higher surface energy. Indeed, the adhesion strength of the Co films after adding 0.03 at.% and 0.06 at.% of W is increased from 35.8 to 43.4 and 56.1 MPa, respectively, concurring well with the respective decrease in the surface energy from 70 to 66 and 60 mJ m^-2 for CoW and CoW _ m. As the added W is further increased to 0.11 at.%, the adhesion strength of the related CoW_h film is reduced to 52.7 MPa, associated with an increase in the surface energy to 69 mJ m ^ - 2. The measured data of CoW_l and CoW_h (high tungsten content) obviously deviates from the inverse variation trend for Co,, CoW l and CoW _ m. This deviation can be attributed to the strong affinity of W for oxygen [41], which likely results in a higher sticking coefficient of W atoms on the SiO₂ substrate compared to Co atoms [42]. This interfacial reaction likely facilitates the formation of tungsten oxide between the CoW_h and S iO_2, thereby enhancing adhesion strength. Such behavior has also been reported in Co-Zr, Co-Al [43] and Co-W-B [44] barriers for Cu metallization. The high concentration of W in CoW_h promotes the diffusion of W atoms and the subsequent formation of tungsten oxide. This process, coupled with the high surface energy of 69 mJ m ^ - 2, results in a moderate adhesion energy of 52.7 MPa. Note that. The data of Table 2 apparently suggest that the magnitude of the adhesion strength, along with the film’s hardness, is a key electromigration-mitigation factor, which in turn places the electromigration-reliability ranking of the four different Co deposits in decreasing order from CoW_m,CoW_h,CoW_l to Co.

text: Grain structure is a crucial factor in defining the strength or weakness of thin solid films. Most noticeably, among the four thin-film materials, CoW_m\(W\=\0.06 at.%) and Co have the best and worst electromigration reliability, respectively. Here, TEM/STEM was used to analyze two narrow lines of CoW_m and Co (the reference sample) after electromigration stressing for a given time at 5.0 × 1 0 ^ 7 ~A~cm ^ - 2 and ambient temperature. The MTFs of Co and CoW_m lines were about 5000 s and 11000 s, respectively. Here, the stressing times of the two Co and CoW_m lines were preset at half of the failure times as 2500 and 5500 s, respectively. Bright-field TEM images were first recorded over broad regions of the two lines along their longitudinal sections, as shown in Fig. 7a and b. It can be seen from Fig. 7a that electrical stressing of the Co line for 2500 s has induced the formation of many dome-shaped voids about 250 nm long and 50−80 nm deep which are located predominantly along the interfaces of the metal line with the surrounding substrate. This situation suggests that electromigration flux divergences of the Co atoms indeed occur at the grain boundaries and interfaces. As shown in the inset of Fig. 7a, prolonged electromigration stressing for 4200 s causes the voids to grow, spreading themselves transversely into open slits with 300−500 nm in length. Subsequently, the line is ruptured at 5000 s. Fig. 7b shows, however, that stressing the CoW_m line for a much longer time of 5500 s only causes the formation of much smaller voids without the formation of any open slits. The imaging analysis suggests again that CoW_m has a better electromigration resistance than Co. It should be noted that the voids in the Co interconnect line are located predominantly along its interfaces with the underlying substrate. It can be inferred from the void location and wear-out profile evolution that, upon electromigration stressing, the depletion of the Co atoms by grain-boundary diffusion starts from the meta / SiO _ 2 interfaces where there probably existing the strongest electron crowding effect and atomic flux divergence [36]. Moreover, the dome-shaped voids display a larger length than depth, suggesting preferential electromigration paths for the Co and W-added Co lines.

This difference was further analyzed by STEM HAADF (high-angle annular dark-field) imaging and high-resolution TEM, as shown in Fig. 7c, d (Co) and Fig.~7e,~f~(CoW_m).. The STEM HAADF image in Fig. 7c shows that the Co line is made of large, columnar crystalline grains. It appears that some grains span the height of the entire interconnect line. The incoming mass flux reaching such ‘blocking’ grains tends to induce a flux divergence that is readily to move upwards along their ‘straight’ grain boundaries to the top free surface, later leading to the formation of large voids in the vicinity of these grains. As seen from the micrograph inserted in Fig. 7a, stressing for 4200 s causes Co atoms to migrate along the interfaces, free surface and grain boundaries, which then accumulate on the top free surface. Eventually, electrical discontinuity in the conductor line leads to open circuit failure.

text: The STEM-HAADF image of the unalloyed Co line (Fig. 7c) exhibits a ‘clean, smooth’ contour, suggesting a relatively low defect density; the line also gives a ‘perfect’ lattice fringe image (Fig. 7d) and [0001] zoneaxis Fourier transform pattern of HCP-Co (inset, Fig. 7d). By contrast, the CoW_m line comprises a stacking of equiaxed grains (Fig. 7b), seemingly offering a more complicated grain structure that could inhibit grain-boundary electromigration. Moreover, the CoW_m line exhibits an HAADF image with an intricate, rough contour (Fig. 7e), suggesting a relatively high defect density. Its high-resolution TEM image (Fig. 7f), taken along the [0001] zone axis, clearly shows the existence of stacking faults on (0001) basal planes, associated with a streaky diffraction pattern of HCP-Co (inset of Fig. 7f). Comparing the unalloyed Co, the equiaxed CoW_m has a more complex grain structure and a higher density of immobile planar defects, which would offer a maze of diffusion routes to retard the void-growth rate.

text: It should be noted that an STEM-HAADF image is produced by col lecting the high-angle scattered electrons due to Rutherford scattering of atomic nuclei using an annulus detector around the principal axis of a primary incident electron beam. The collected signals are thus highly sensitive to the variation in the atomic number of the atoms in the imaged specimen, as opposed to the conventional TEM dark-field imaging method which utilizes extremely small-angle Bragg diffracted electrons. The high dependence of imaging contrast on atomic number makes STEM-HAADF a facile way to resolve a higher atomic-number alloy from its matrix material, as for the case of the W in Co matrix. However, using STEM-HAADF imaging, high-resolution TEM and STEM-EDX line scanning/mapping turned out to be inconclusive regarding the location of the added W, indicating that 0.06 at.% of W could be beyond the detection limit of the Talos™ F200X microscope.

text: An all-wet SAM-seeding and electroless-plating process has been developed to form thin films of Co and extremely diluted CoW alloys with controlled thin-film properties, including deposition rates, alloy compositions, deposit surface morphologies and microstructure stability against thermal stressing. We then extend this all-wet process to fill these metal films into SiO 2 trenches, eventually fabricating nanolines of three different CoW alloys for electromigration-behavior evaluations, using nanolines of Co as a reference. The electromigration mitigation for all three nanolines of Co alloys with 0.03 at.%, 0.06 at.% and 0.11 at.% of added W, termed CoW_l,CoW_m and CoW_h, respectively, under accelerated current stressing conditions of the order of 10^7A cm ^ - 2 has been confirmed. Most noticeably, the CoW_m line containing a moderate amount of W, while only 0.06 at.%, yields a significantly reduced current density scaling factor of 0.33, which is much smaller than that of the Co line (0.50). So, it also yields a much slower void growth rate, associated with an electromigration lifetime at least twice as long as that of the Co line. While a variety of advanced TEM analyses fail to locate the trace amount of W which is less than one atom in about 1000 cobaltmatrix atoms, the 0.06 at% added W markedly elevates the adhesion strength and hardness of Co from 35.8 to 56.1 MPa and 14.8 to 17.5 μN nm ^ - 1, respectively. Moreover, it also reduces Co surface energy from 70 to 60 mJ m ^ - 2, favoring the wetting of the electroless deposits onto the underlying substrate. A fourth benefit given by the optimum W content, as found from advanced STEM/TEM analysis, is that the big electromigration-accelerating blocking grains, as exist in the Co line, are absent from the CoW_m line. The full account of the thin-film properties being investigated correlates well with the reliability performance of the four different metallic thin films/interconnects under thermal/electricfield stressing. It also reasonably explains why the ranking of their electromigration reliability being increased from Co, CoW (0.03 at.%), CoW_h (0.11 at.%) to CoW_m (0.06 at.%).
